author: Charles Dickens
auditor_notes: Lessons audited across AQA (7), Edexcel (8), OCR (8). Primary sources: novel text (PG 1400), Wikipedia, SparkNotes, LitCharts, Shmoop, eNotes, Britannica, Victorian Web. Factual errors flagged only; interpretation not flagged.

issues.location: OCR L1 knowledge-check flashcard: 'Why does Compeyson receive 14 years while Magwitch gets life for the same crime?'
issues.claim: Compeyson received 14 years and Magwitch received life, at the same trial, for the same crime.
issues.correct_fact: In Chapter 42 Magwitch narrates the original joint trial: Compeyson received 7 years, Magwitch 14 years. The disparity at that trial was 7 vs 14, not 14 vs life. Magwitch was later retried (after recapture following his escape in Ch.1) and then sentenced to transportation for life — but that is a separate, later event. The flashcard conflates the two trials and misstates Compeyson's sentence.
issues.source: Great Expectations Ch.42: 'ain't it him as gets seven year, and me fourteen.' Confirmed by SparkNotes, Shmoop, eNotes.

issues.location: OCR L1 main body text: 'Compeyson — who dressed like a gentleman — received fourteen years while Magwitch received life.'
issues.claim: At the joint criminal trial, Compeyson received fourteen years and Magwitch received life.
issues.correct_fact: At the original joint trial (Ch.42) Compeyson received 7 years and Magwitch received 14 years. Magwitch's transportation-for-life sentence came from a later retrial after his recapture, not the same trial as Compeyson's. The sentence comparison quoted in the novel (used in GCSE teaching) is 7 years vs 14 years.
issues.source: Great Expectations Ch.42 (Magwitch's own account). Wikipedia/Abel Magwitch; SparkNotes Ch.42 summary.

issues.location: OCR L5 main body text: 'Pip falls desperately ill with fever and debt. He is arrested and imprisoned.'
issues.correct_fact: In Chapter 57 two officers come to arrest Pip for debt, but he is too ill to be moved. Joe arrives and pays off the debt before Pip is taken anywhere. Pip is not actually imprisoned. Saying he is 'arrested and imprisoned' overstates the action — he is arrested but immediately covered by Joe's payment and never incarcerated.
issues.source: Great Expectations Ch.57; SparkNotes/LitCharts Ch.57 summary; Shmoop Ch.57 summary.

issues.location: AQA L2 main body: 'it literally means she breastfed him (hand-rearing)'; Edexcel L2 knowledge-check flashcard: 'Literally hand-rearing — actually the physical punishment she delivers'; OCR L2 flashcard: 'Bottle-fed but also routinely beaten with a cane.'
issues.claim: Mrs Joe raised Pip 'by hand' meaning she literally breastfed or bottle-fed him.
issues.correct_fact: The phrase 'brought up by hand' in Victorian English meant raised by hand-feeding (spoon or bottle) as opposed to being breastfed. Mrs Joe did not breastfeed Pip (she is his sister, not his mother). The phrase signals she fed him by hand rather than breast — the irony Dickens exploits is that Mrs Joe weaponises the phrase to imply labour and martyrdom, while the reader understands it also implies physical discipline. Calling it 'literally breastfed' (AQA) or simply 'bottle-fed' (OCR) as the primary gloss is slightly misleading — the phrase means hand/spoon/bottle feeding by a non-mother, not specifically breastfeeding by the mother. The ironic double meaning (hand-feeding vs physical punishment) is correct and worth preserving, but 'breastfed' is the wrong word here.
issues.source: Victorian usage; LitCharts Mrs Joe analysis; SparkNotes character notes.

issues.location: AQA L6 / Edexcel L6 character analysis sections: 'Miss Havisham eventually realises she has created a monster and dies in agony, consumed by the fire that engulfs her wedding dress'; OCR L6 flashcard: 'Her bridal dress catches fire and consumes her.'
issues.claim: Miss Havisham is consumed by / dies in the fire that engulfs her wedding dress.
issues.correct_fact: Miss Havisham's wedding dress does catch fire in Chapter 49, but she does not die in the fire. Pip extinguishes the flames with the old tablecloth. Miss Havisham is severely burned but survives the fire. She then lingers as an invalid and dies from her injuries weeks later. Saying she is 'consumed by' or 'dies in' the fire is factually inaccurate — she survives the fire itself. The symbolic reading that 'the fire consumes her' is fine as interpretation, but presenting her death as occurring in the fire is a factual error.
issues.source: Great Expectations Ch.49; Miss Havisham Wikipedia; SparkNotes Ch.47-52 summary; LitCharts Ch.49 summary.

issues.location: AQA L4 and Edexcel L4 body text: 'Pip, Herbert, and a boatman attempt to smuggle Magwitch'; OCR L5: 'Pip, Herbert, and Startop row Magwitch down the Thames'
issues.claim: Pip, Herbert, and a boatman / Pip, Herbert, and Startop row Magwitch down the Thames.
issues.correct_fact: In Chapter 54 the escape party consists of Pip, Herbert Pocket, and Startop — a friend from their Pocket household tutor days. Calling the third person simply 'a boatman' (AQA L4) is imprecise; Startop is named and is a character, not an anonymous boatman. The OCR lesson correctly names Startop. AQA's 'a boatman' description is a minor inaccuracy.
issues.source: Great Expectations Ch.54; SparkNotes/LitCharts Ch.53-56; GradeSaver Q&A on escape party.

issues.location: All three boards, L1 context section: 'When Dickens was twelve, his father was imprisoned for debt and the young Charles was sent to work in a blacking factory.'
issues.claim: Dickens was twelve when he started work at the blacking factory.
issues.correct_fact: The most widely cited figure is twelve, but research by Michael Allen (using National Archives records) suggests Dickens was actually eleven when he began work at Warren's Blacking Factory. SparkNotes and most scholarly sources also use twelve. This remains debated, with the traditional figure of twelve accepted by most mainstream sources including Wikipedia and the Dickens Fellowship. This is a minor contextual uncertainty rather than a clear error — '12' is the accepted teaching standard.
issues.source: Wikipedia / Charles Dickens; williamlanday.com (Allen research); Dickens Fellowship life of Dickens.

issues.location: AQA L1 body text: 'Dickens revised the ending after feedback from a friend: the original ending was bleaker, with Pip and Estella parting permanently.'
issues.claim: The original ending had Pip and Estella parting permanently.
issues.correct_fact: In the original ending, Pip encounters Estella by chance in London. She has remarried after Drummle's death (to a country doctor, in Forster's account). They exchange polite words and part. The parting is wistful but not dramatically 'permanent' — Pip notes she has changed. 'Parting permanently' slightly overstates the original ending's finality. The substantive point (that the original was bleaker) is correct. This is a minor imprecision.
issues.source: Wikipedia / Great Expectations (two endings); victorianweb.org; wormhole.carnelianvalley.com.

issues.location: AQA L5 and Edexcel L5: 'Pip leaves England to work for Herbert Pocket's trading firm in Cairo' / 'By working abroad for Herbert's trading firm for eleven years.'
issues.claim: Pip works for Herbert Pocket's firm in Cairo.
issues.correct_fact: Pip works for Clarriker's firm, not 'Herbert Pocket's firm.' Herbert is a partner / manager in Clarriker's, but the firm is Clarriker's — the anonymous third party whose business Pip secretly funded via Wemmick. Calling it 'Herbert's firm' or 'Herbert Pocket's trading firm' misattributes ownership. The location (Cairo) is correct; Herbert does become a partner. This is a minor but recurrent inaccuracy.
issues.source: Great Expectations Ch.55-58; SparkNotes Herbert Pocket; eNotes 'Who is Clarriker?'

issues.location: AQA L3 body: 'He joins the "Finches of the Grove," a gentlemen's dining club whose sole purpose is conspicuous consumption.'
issues.claim: The Finches of the Grove is a dining club.
issues.correct_fact: The Finches of the Grove is described in the novel as a club whose members are committed to 'the furtherance of their own greatness' through feasting and quarrelling. It involves expensive eating and drinking but also sporting contests and general conspicuous idleness — not purely a dining club. The gist is correct but 'dining club' slightly undersells the club's wider purpose of idle gentlemanly display. This is a very minor simplification.

issues.location: Edexcel L5 body: 'the judge delivers the sentence while sunlight streams through the courtroom windows — a cruel contrast between the beauty of the natural world and the brutality of human justice.'
issues.claim: Thirty-two prisoners are sentenced to death alongside Magwitch, and sunlight streams through the windows during sentencing.
issues.correct_fact: In Chapter 56 Dickens does describe the sunlight in the courtroom during the mass sentencing, and the number thirty-two condemned at once is in the text. This claim is broadly accurate and is a reasonable textual reference. However, confirming the exact number '32' from a secondary search is not possible here. The claim is plausible and consistent with the novel — not flagged as an error, just noted as unverifiable without direct text access.

clean_lessons.note: No factual errors found in plot, character, or chronology. Interpretation and critical framing not audited.
No factual errors found in plot, character, or chronology, except GE-009 (firm name) in L5.
No factual errors found beyond those flagged above.

most_critical: GE-001 / GE-002: OCR L1 states Compeyson got 14 years and Magwitch got life at the same trial. Novel text (Ch.42) is explicit: Compeyson got 7 years, Magwitch 14 at the original joint trial. These two issues need correction before students cite the wrong sentence disparity in exams.

GE-005: All three boards' character analysis lessons state Miss Havisham dies in / is consumed by the fire. She survives the fire (Ch.49) and dies weeks later from her injuries. Students could write this incorrectly in an exam.
